en: Two connected passed pawns on the 6th rank, kings too far to take part: they beat an ENTIRE rook. One rank earlier (5th), it's the reverse — the rook always holds. The exact threshold comes down to one square of advance.
Push right away, without hesitating
Hesitate, and lose it all
The first pawn races toward promotion — the rook can only stop one at a time.
A king move that looks harmless — tuck the king away before pushing. But every tempo counts: Black's king uses it to get closer.
The second pawn follows — now both threaten to promote, and the rook can no longer cover both squares.

The rook can only watch, powerless, as one of the two pawns inevitably promotes. From the root, every Black try the oracle tested failed the same way: a lone rook never covers two promotion squares at once.
Black's king rushes toward the pawns. The 6th-rank threshold no longer suffices once the defending king has time to join the fight — the lost tempo flipped the entire verdict.

A rook is worth more than two pawns — on paper. But a rook can only be on one square at a time, and two well-advanced connected pawns offer it two at once. On the 6th rank, it's already too late for the rook.
The 6th rank: already lost for the rook
The white king comes to shepherd his pawns — they barely need him for the essential part, but he keeps Black's king from any incursion.
The rook looks for an angle — but she can only aim at ONE pawn per move, and there's always another one free to advance.
The rook switches targets: she just lost a tempo the second pawn happily banks.
She finally eats one — inevitable from the start, and it isn't enough: the other is already on the 7th.
A queen appears — the rook was never equipped to stop BOTH pawns. Two connected pawns on the 6th cannot be held by a single piece.

Simple opposition isn't enough here: Black's king must answer EVERY move of White's king with the one precise square that corresponds to it — one out of seven. All the others lose, some more than 40 moves later with nothing on the board to hint at it.
The right square, move after move
One square off, and it's all lost
White's king sets off — which square must Black's king answer with?

The only square that holds. Of the seven legal moves available here, six lose — some more than forty moves later, with no visible hint giving it away for a long time. This is exactly what "corresponding square" means: b3 on the board answers to c5, and to no other square.
A square that looks just as reasonable as c5 — same direction, same general idea of staying close. And yet: it loses.
White's king continues its manoeuvre.
And Black's king answers correctly again. The pair changes (c3 now answers to d5), but the principle stays: one square, and only one, preserves the draw at each moment.

White's king infiltrates through the square that Kc6 left unanswered — and nothing stops it from here. The difference between draw and loss came down to ONE square, invisible unless you know the exact correspondence.

Two passed pawns one file apart, a white king at the far end of the board, and yet Black is lost. Black's king can touch neither: approaching one means stepping out of the other's square. They guard each other — hence the name.
Touch one, and the other runs
The other side of the mirror
Pushing with check is giving the pawn away
Trying to save both
Black's king comes for c3.
Black's king steps between the two pawns.
THE move. White does not try to save c3: he launches the other one. Black's king now faces a choice that isn't one — take on c3, or chase the a-pawn. He cannot do both.
The human reflex: you don't drop a pawn for nothing, so the king sets off to defend it. Except that he is seven squares away — and the a-pawn will never set off by itself.
Black's king collects. Count the a4 pawn's square from c3: he is already outside it, and every step toward a8 arrives one tempo late.

Queening, with Black's king two squares away. The c3 pawn was no gift: it was the bait. Remember the ONE-file gap — side by side, Black's king would stop both; further apart, he would not even have had to choose.

WAIT. Neither pawn can advance — Black's king would take it. But he has to move, and every square brings him closer to one pawn, hence further from the other. White's king, far away, is merely passing the turn.

With check, hence irresistible — and losing. From b5, Black's king TOUCHES a4: the pawn does not arrive there, it surrenders there. The rule that governs this whole ending fits in one line: never push a pawn onto a square the enemy king already covers.
The king picks the a-pawn. He attacks it, and thinks he is gaining a tempo.
Exactly the move from chapter 1, mirrored: the attacked pawn is abandoned, the OTHER one runs. Nothing more to remember — the theme does not care which file it happens on.
Same queen, same two-square gap. The two pawns are interchangeable: it is Black's king who decides, by approaching, which of them will queen.
The pawn falls. One is left, alone, with White's king at the far end of the board: that is a draw, and it was a win.
Too late for the second one. Black's king is inside its square and catches it without effort — a lone pawn does not queen against a king who can see it.
The pawn falls anyway, and the lost tempo never comes back.
The same move as in chapter 1, one tempo too late. Count the square: from c3, Black's king is INSIDE it — whereas he was outside when a4 went at once. A single tempo separates the win from the draw.

Black's king is cut off from the pawn — no Philidor position possible. The rook instead posts itself on the promotion rank (the file doesn't matter) and simply waits: the moment the pawn arrives, it's captured.
Waiting on the right rank
The check from behind, given too soon
White's pawn advances, escorted by its king.
The exact square on the 8th rank doesn't matter — what counts is being there, ready to intercept the pawn whichever file it lands on.
The check from behind is often the key resource against a king-supported pawn — but given now, far too early, it only helps White's king get closer to its pawn.
The rook can even harass the pawn from the side along the way, as long as it keeps time to return to the promotion rank.

Back just in time on the 8th rank. The pawn can promote — the rook, already stationed on that rank, will recapture it at once. Verified draw: no White try the oracle tested from this crossroads ever did better.
White's king advances without fear — Black's rook wasted its check, and the king will now escort the pawn all the way home.

Grigoriev, 1930: two pawns against one, everyone in the queenside corner — and the ONLY winning path goes through h8, at the far end of the world. Sixteen king moves there and back to steal an opposition. The finest demonstration ever composed of what “going the other way” means.
The grand detour
The mirror push
The king leaves unprepared
The corner stalemate
The broken mirror
The only first move: preparing c4 while conceding nothing. The mirror push 1.b4? lets the draw in (see that chapter), and so does moving the king first.
A passed pawn at once — what could be more natural? But this pawn is judged by what it locks in:
Step out first, push later? Move order is the whole study:
The best defence: watching b4 while threatening …b4 himself. The white king seems to have nothing but poisoned squares…
…except one. 2.b4+? Ka6! draws, and the natural 2.Ka7? or 2.Kb7? walks into a gorgeous STALEMATE (its own chapter). The king takes the only clean exit: the eighth rank.
The “normal” exit — and the study's hidden jewel:
The trade is done: the c-pawn is passed, but the black king holds the corridor opposition — b6 against b8 — planning …Kc5-b4 the moment the white king comes near.
The mirror: each white step along the eighth rank is answered directly opposite along the sixth, the c-pawn never out of sight.

The study's outrageous move: the winning king locks himself into the most godforsaken corner of the board. But watch the mirror: 9…Kh6?? would break it — c5! and the pawn runs (see “The broken mirror”). The black king must stay on the f-file.
Forced, keeping guard over c5. And the theft is done: the kings now stand h8-f6 — the old direct opposition has vanished into the corner.
Following to the end of the world — the mirror reflex. But from h6 the black king no longer covers c5:
The descent begins: rank by rank, the white king pins his counterpart to the h/f duet.
The next-to-last rung, and the finest: 14…Kf3? would lose touch with c5 — c5! decides. The black king must climb back, finally conceding the third rank.
Look what has changed: g3 against f5 — it is the WHITE king who owns the lateral opposition now. The march back west will be a victory parade.

And the mirror dies its beautiful death: 18…Kd5 is forbidden by the c4-pawn! Next come Kd4, c5 and Kc4 — the pawn is escorted home. Thirty-five half-moves, a round trip to h8, to win ONE tempo: this one.
…his own king. No more b3-c4 to open a road, no exit via a7/b7 under the black king's eye: the a6-b6 shuttle keeps house forever. Tablebase verdict: draw — the preparatory 1.b3! was no luxury.
The liquidation forces the draw — nothing to win will remain. And beware of worse:
Declining the trade LOSES: the b-pawn runs b3-b2-b1 while the white pawns watch. 2.cxb4 was forced — a dead draw, the doubled b-pawns win nothing here.
Unstoppable. So the study held all three verdicts: one win (b3!), draws, and even a loss for the “winning” side.

Look at the black king: a4 and b5 taken by the pawns, a6 and b6 by the king — STALEMATE. The same drowning awaits 2.Kb7?. Only 2.Kb8!, one rank higher, leaves a6 and b6 breathing: that is why the grand detour starts from the exact corner.

…and the pawn is off: c6, c7, c8=Q, three tempi the black king, stuck on the h-side, will never claw back. That is why 9.Kh8! was riskless: the duel was never king against king, but the black king against THIS push.

One e-pawn, one h-pawn each, and four White tries that all look alike. Only one wins — the other three, including pushing the pawn, only draw. The technique that follows is the longest in the whole module: 61 moves to conversion.
The only move that wins
Pushing the pawn right away?

The only one of four tries that wins. Pushing right away (e3, e4+) or tucking the king on g2/h2 look just as active — and yet each one only draws. The plan, once launched: advance the e-pawn, abandon it at the right moment, then race the king to keep Black's king away from h8, its drawing corner.
Seems logical: create a passed pawn without waiting. But with check, Black's king captures it at once, and not a trace remains of the king march that was doing all the work.
Black's king advances too — it has nothing better to offer.
White's king continues its route toward the queenside, where its presence will matter far more than the h-pawn's.
Same idea throughout: the king makes progress while Black's king only has waiting moves to offer.
The pawn falls, and with it every winning chance — the position flattens straight into a draw. The king had to clear the road before the pawn advanced, never the other way round.

Horwitz and Kling believed, in 1851, that a fortress existed here for the knight's side. There isn't one — it's a general win, confirmed up to 78 moves by tablebases. The full technique is reputed to be one of the longest and least intuitive in all of chess; this course shows only the very first choice that launches it.
The very first step of a 63-move technique
A square that looks safe isn't

White's king approaches the knight — the starting point of a technique so long it could never be found without a machine before the tablebase era. What this course keeps is only this: contrary to what Horwitz and Kling believed, there is NO square where the knight's side can simply settle in and hold.
A bishop retreat that looks harmless, keeping control of the dark squares. And yet: a draw, where almost everything else wins.

A king, a bishop and a knight, without a single pawn, hold a draw against a lone queen — the only known configuration of its kind. The key: the bishop stays on g2, where it guards both the king and the knight posted just in front of it.
The bishop never leaves g2
The bishop must stay: move it, and the knight falls
The king stays in the corner, sheltered — the queen can approach all it likes, it never finds a way in.
A simple side-step is enough to parry the check, without ever needing to move the bishop or the knight. Verified draw: no Black try the oracle tested from this crossroads ever did better.
A square that looks just as safe to parry the check — the bishop blocks the back rank. But it abandons the defence of the knight on e4 at the same time.
The queen grabs the knight for free. Without it, there's no fortress left — king and bishop alone can do nothing against the queen.

An extra kingside pawn, rooks still on the board: the temptation is to manoeuvre, to gain ground piece in hand. And yet the only road to the full point is to TRADE EVERYTHING — the majority only speaks once it's a pure pawn ending.
Trade to let the pawn speak
Keep the rooks? Only a draw
The only move that wins — and it consists of giving up right away what could be kept. Once the rooks are gone, no tactical resource can save the side down a pawn: only square-counting remains.

The reflex: manoeuvre, activate the rook, rush nothing. And the result suffers for it: WITHOUT the trade, Black's rook always finds enough activity and checks to hold — the pawn majority alone isn't enough while heavy pieces complicate matters.
A king race now — exactly the terrain where an extra pawn converts cleanly.
The white king takes the decisive opposition while Black's king was busy elsewhere — the g3/f3 preparation just paid off.
Breakthrough. From here, the “Breakthrough” course takes over — the extra pawn manufactures a passer Black's king can no longer catch.
Black answers with rook activity that neutralises everything — count White's tries from this crossroads: none ever did better than a draw.
A lone knight can blockade a pawn forever — but ONLY if it gets in front of it in time. This ending almost always comes down to one race: the pawn, or the defending knight?
The defender is too far: run
Bring the king first? Too late
The ONLY move that wins — any king move, even to “help”, gives the black knight time to rush back and blockade. Black's knight and king are too far: this is a race, and races are won by starting now.
The cautious reflex — and it costs the entire win. Black's knight now has EXACTLY enough time to get back in front of the pawn.
The knight rushes over, but he is missing exactly the tempo a cautious white king would have handed him.
Still one move behind.
One more queen, one lonely knight: the conversion is now a formality.
The knight races for the key square c5, which watches the queening square.

Fork on king and pawn: the knight arrives just in time and picks up the pawn on the way through. Drawn — for the sake of a SINGLE tempo lost on move one. And had Black's knight already held the square in front of the pawn from the start, no white manoeuvre would ever have changed a thing: a well-placed knight in front of a lone pawn is a fortress, not a temporary obstacle.

One pawn on each wing, both well advanced, against a lone knight: its limited range — several moves to cross the board — keeps it from covering both queening squares at once. Push now: waste a single tempo and the knight has time to pick its target.
The a-pawn races toward promotion — the knight can't deal with it without abandoning the other wing.
A king move that looks harmless — get to safety before pushing. But the knight takes advantage at once.
Almost queening. The knight, busy here, no longer has time to cross the whole board for the other pawn.
White's king comes to help while the second pawn, on h5, waits its turn in reserve. Won: verified from the root, only the two pawn pushes held the win — every king move only drew.
The knight grabs the a-pawn for free — the lost tempo gave it exactly the time it needed. Only the h-pawn is left, and a lone knight can handle that: a draw.

A lone knight, its king nowhere in sight, against king and rook's pawn: a draw — as long as the pawn has not passed its 6th rank. But the defence hangs by a thread: after every white king attack, the tablebase gives exactly ONE saving move, always the same motif — a knight check that buys the time to come back. A dance step worth knowing by heart.
The c8-d6-b5 dance — one saving move, every time
What if the pawn pushes? It falls
Ne7 — one square too far
White's only idea: evict the knight from its blockading post. While it camps on a7, the pawn literally cannot move.

The ONLY saving move (everything else loses, tablebase-checked) — and it is a check. The knight never defends passively: it bites as it retreats, and the check buys the tempo it will need to come back.
